From this we can draw a broader conclusion.
The question of the person who commits a major sin first entered the arena as part of a political struggle. Only afterward did it move into the arena of theoretical and intellectual debate.
The same applies to Muʿāwiya’s position toward ʿAlī.
Muʿāwiya had spent twenty years as governor in Syria building the political position that would later support his ambitions.
But he could not openly pursue those ambitions without a justification.
He therefore used the same argument: ʿAlī was responsible for the blood of ʿUthmān, and anyone who took part in shedding the blood of a Muslim was a killer and therefore guilty of a major sin.
This, in turn, was used to justify rebelling against ʿAlī as caliph, fighting him, and eventually even challenging him for the caliphate itself, as Muʿāwiya ultimately did.
There was also another group of Companions who opposed ʿAlī politically, though less sharply than Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, and Muʿāwiya.
Their ambitions did not go as far as seeking the caliphate for themselves.
Their position on the person who commits a major sin therefore reflected a more middle-ground political position.
Among them were Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, Muḥammad ibn Maslama, Usāma ibn Zayd, and others like them.
They refused to support ʿAlī in the conflict, but at the same time they also refused to fight him.
Al-Aḥnaf ibn Qays did the same in Basra, together with six thousand men under his command. Some members of the Azd tribe took a similar position.

Why did these men remain neutral during a conflict such as the Battle of the Camel, even though some of them could see the fighting with their own eyes and others were close enough to hear directly about it?
As leading Muslims and influential figures, the conflict concerned them. They might normally have been expected to enter it on one side or the other.
There is no doubt that political considerations lay behind their position.
But they could not appear before the wider Muslim community as neutral without giving any reason beyond their own political calculations.
That would not only have failed to persuade the public. It would also have exposed their political motives.
So once again, the issue of the person who commits a major sin appears.

There was a claim that ʿAlī was among those responsible for killing ʿUthmān—that is, a claim that he had committed one of the major sins. They could then tell the public that they were uncertain about the whole matter: they had no firm view on whether ʿAlī really was a killer, or on whether someone who committed murder—one of the major sins—should be fought with weapons or put to death. In other words, these “neutral” people justified their neutrality by saying they were unsure how to judge someone who committed a major sin. And being unsure in one’s judgment, just like reaching a firm judgment, was itself a form of independent reasoning. A Muslim had the right to form such a judgment and act on it.

Finally, what we want to show is this: the reason intellectual debate at the time became so absorbed first in the question of the person who commits a major sin, and then in the meaning of faith, was originally the political conflict over the caliphate—especially the different positions people took toward ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya.

The Kharijites insisted that anyone who committed a major sin was an unbeliever, and that actions were part of faith itself. From this, they concluded that they had to fight both ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya. This gave them a justification for the position they had taken after the arbitration at Ṣiffīn. The Shiʿa fought hard against the Kharijite theory because they knew that behind it lay an attack on Imam ʿAlī’s position, and even on the validity of his faith. Sunni scholars who also opposed the Kharijite view were, in practice, defending every Muslim caliph whom that theory condemned or discredited.

We do not deny that, during the intense debate surrounding it, the question of the person who commits a major sin—and the related question of what faith means—gradually developed an intellectual life of its own. It moved away from the immediate political conflict, or at least made those political positions harder to see.

Of course we do not deny this. But recognizing an intellectual phenomenon in its own right does not mean treating it as cut off from the political and social roots to which it is objectively connected, whether we want that connection to exist or not. Nor should the intellectual form of the debate prevent historians from seeing those roots or from examining the connection between them and the ideas that grew from them.
In Chapter Three of Part One, we saw how closely the historical development of Arab thought was connected with the political events surrounding the struggle over the caliphate after the Prophet.

By the final years of the Rightly Guided Caliphate—after the killing of ʿUthmān and the accession of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib under the system of consultation for which ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb had laid the practical foundation—it was already clear that this struggle was moving toward something new. Political divisions were beginning to develop into distinct schools and movements with their own theories, or their own “ideologies,” if we may use the term.

This became clear as positions toward ʿAlī’s caliphate began to take shape. Some of the Companions refused to pledge allegiance to him but did not go so far as to fight him. Others also refused allegiance and openly called for war against him. They then fought him in the Battle of the Camel at Basra and at Ṣiffīn.

At the head of this second camp stood ʿĀʾisha, daughter of Abū Bakr and wife of the Prophet, followed by Muʿāwiya ibn Abī Sufyān. At the time, Muʿāwiya governed Syria on behalf of the third caliph, ʿUthmān. He represented the economically dominant class in Syria and the leading Umayyad families. A third group supported ʿAlī. Most of them came from Iraq, especially Kufa.
From this point on, Arab-Islamic society began to divide into different tendencies and “ideologies.”

But if we wanted to understand the social roots of these divisions, we first had to return to the political and social setting in which they developed. It was there that they gradually took shape, acquired theoretical forms, and eventually became part of a much wider intellectual movement. Within that movement lay the earliest seeds of philosophical thought, which would later become a relatively independent field of philosophy in its own right.

The political and social setting we have in mind is the Umayyad period: the Arab-Islamic society ruled by the new state founded by Muʿāwiya, the first Umayyad ruler after the Rightly Guided Caliphs to take the title of caliph.

It was in this setting that the Shiʿa and the Kharijites emerged as the first two clearly distinct sects in Islam. Each developed its own view of political authority and the caliphate, as well as its own ideas about faith and knowledge. For that reason, we devoted the first chapter of this second part of our study to these two movements.
But before we could place the Shiʿa and Kharijites within the Umayyad world, we first had to give a clear picture of that world itself.
At the beginning of that picture, we drew attention to two features that marked Umayyad rule from the time of its founder, Muʿāwiya.

The first was the revival of tribal loyalties. Muʿāwiya strengthened his rule by allying with the Kalb tribes against the Qays tribes—the two main branches into which the Arabs were traditionally divided by ancestry. He hoped to give his new state a firm base in Arab tribal loyalty that could serve as its main protection against future upheavals.
The second feature was class division.

We reached this conclusion by examining the social order in Syria when Muʿāwiya governed it on behalf of the third Rightly Guided Caliph. The same basic social order continued to develop after Muʿāwiya became an independent ruler and founded the Umayyad state and caliphate.

This social order was feudal in character and had been inherited from the Sasanian and Byzantine periods. The Umayyads, with Muʿāwiya at their head, added something new that further strengthened the power of the landed elite. Muʿāwiya and his family themselves became major landowners. They used both slaves and free workers in agriculture and employed local specialists to organize farming and irrigation.

In this way, a new Arab Umayyad aristocracy of landowners emerged and allied itself with the existing local landed elite. It also formed alliances with major merchants and local Christian clergy against Christian clergy connected with the Byzantine Church.
Umayyad society therefore contained both a tribal alliance and a class alliance.

But the tribal alliance adapted itself to the class alliance, so no direct contradiction developed between the two. The allied tribes received special privileges, and over time these privileges themselves took on a class character.

When wealth becomes concentrated in this way, the result is predictable. A deep divide gradually opens between, on one side, those who hold economic and political power through the landed system, and on the other, the people who work the land, small craftsmen, and slaves.

Under the Umayyads, this process eventually reached an extreme point. The state placed a very heavy burden on the productive forces of society through taxation and harsh tax collection. This led to repeated uprisings in different parts of the Umayyad realm.

These uprisings also had intellectual effects. As we put it earlier in this chapter, they “brought the developing movement of Arab thought, in the late seventh and early eighth centuries, face to face with social and political reality.”

We discussed the most important of these uprisings in order to see how they were reflected in thought, and how those intellectual responses were connected with the social and political reality that produced them. Among them were Shiʿi uprisings and the uprisings of the Turks and the Kharijites, together with the forces that lay behind each.
The Shiʿa were the first to rise against Umayyad power, at the beginning of the reign of Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya, the first heir to Muʿāwiya’s throne.
After giving a fairly detailed picture of the Umayyad setting in which the Shiʿa and Kharijites emerged as distinct movements, we turned to the positions and theories of each.
In discussing the Shiʿa, we began by defining the political and intellectual character of the Shiʿi position. From there, we moved to the theory that grew out of it.

The first was that the Shiʿa’s attitude toward ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, despite the differences among their various branches, expressed a political position toward different rulers of the Islamic caliphates. In most cases, this position was one of opposition.
The second was that this political opposition often also had a social character.

By this we mean that Shiʿi opposition was not limited to the form of government or to the people who ruled. It was often also directed against the way rulers treated weaker and oppressed social classes and groups.

We traced this social position to the fact that most ordinary Shiʿa themselves had suffered persecution throughout Arab-Islamic political history, as had their imams and leaders. It was therefore natural that they should also be affected by the persecution suffered by other weak groups in their society.

When we turned to Shiʿi theory itself, we tried to identify its earliest foundations, apart from the later developments and new ideas that appeared after the Shiʿa divided into a number of different sects.
We concluded that the basic ideas shared by the different Shiʿi branches were these:
First, political authority in Islam is a divine right. Authority belongs to God, not to the Muslim community.
Second, since authority belongs to God, the community does not have the right to choose the person who will hold it.

Third, God chose ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib as the designated successor, imam, and caliph after Muḥammad, and chose ʿAlī’s descendants after him. The different Shiʿi branches disagree over the exact line of succession among those descendants.
Fourth, the imamate—or caliphate—is a basic part of Shiʿi Islamic belief.

Not long after the first appearance of the Shiʿa, a more extreme group emerged whose view of ʿAlī raised him above the level of ordinary human beings. Some went even further and gave him divine qualities. These became known as the extremist Shiʿa, the ghulāt.

The more moderate Shiʿa continued to regard ʿAlī as an imam protected from error, much as the Prophet was protected from error. They also regarded him as the best and most knowledgeable person of his time. The same qualities were then applied to the imams descended from him: each was regarded as protected from error, and as the best and most knowledgeable person of his own age.

These more extreme ideas entered Shiʿi theory through the development of theological and philosophical debate, once that kind of thinking began to dominate sectarian thought and the questions raised by political conflict.

From al-Shahrastānī’s description of the doctrines of the extremist Shiʿa—al-Shahrastānī being one of the great historians of philosophy—we concluded that ideas such as divine indwelling, the transmigration of souls, and similar doctrines that had been prominent in Persian and Indian philosophy entered the beliefs of these groups.

In our discussion of the extremist Shiʿa, we also examined the doctrine of the Kaysāniyya, one of their branches. Here, for the first time in the history of Arab-Islamic thought, we find beliefs in divine indwelling and in rajʿa—the return to earthly life after death.
We also identified a class element in this movement: it was closely connected with a group of mawālī, non-Arab clients attached to Arab tribes.
After that, we discussed the Shiʿi “theory” of knowledge in general.

Our conclusion was that, for the Shiʿa, knowledge remained connected with a divine source. It came from God to the Prophet through revelation, and from the Prophet to the infallible imam whom God had appointed through the Prophet.

At the same time, however, we placed great value on the emergence of ijtihād, or independent legal reasoning, in Islamic law. This movement led to the development of a rational discipline: uṣūl al-fiqh, the study of the principles used to derive Islamic law.
In it we found a real effort to organize knowledge in a systematic way. We also found a move beyond the rigid abstract form of Aristotelian logic when drawing conclusions from premises.

Alongside this was another important feature: the tendency to treat thought as an interconnected whole. This can be seen clearly in the way the different Arab-Islamic sciences overlapped with one another—for example, the close relationship between uṣūl al-fiqh and rational theological debate.
In our discussion of the Kharijites, we first examined the historical origins of their movement.

At the beginning, they fought in ʿAlī’s army against Muʿāwiya at the Battle of Ṣiffīn. They then “withdrew” from ʿAlī’s ranks in anger after he accepted the idea of arbitration. That arbitration ended in a carefully arranged maneuver meant to remove ʿAlī from the caliphate while leaving Muʿāwiya in place.
The Kharijites justified their break with ʿAlī by developing a new theory of faith.

For them, faith had two parts: belief, and action in accordance with that belief. This led them to declare ʿAlī, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, ʿĀʾisha, Muʿāwiya, and all later Umayyad and Abbasid rulers unbelievers. In their view, all of them acted against what was right, and therefore none of them could truly be believers.
On the basis of this theory, the Kharijites saw themselves as obliged to fight anyone who departed from the truth—which, in their words, was “God’s right, not the right of men.”

Their history was therefore filled with bloody violence, which was answered with violence in return, whether from the Shiʿa or the Umayyads. The greatest blow against them came when al-Ḥajjāj ibn Yūsuf al-Thaqafī took control of Iraq on behalf of the Umayyad caliph ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.
Yet when we examined their principles in the abstract, we also found a positive side.
Unlike both the Sunnis and the Shiʿa, the Kharijites did not limit the caliphate to ʿAlī’s family, as the Shiʿa did, or to branches of Quraysh, as the Sunnis did.

They argued that the caliph did not have to be a Hāshimite or even a member of Quraysh. He could even be an Abyssinian slave. The caliphate, they said, belonged to the community, and the community had the right to choose whoever was worthy of carrying this responsibility and protecting Muslim interests, regardless of tribe, ethnicity, or class.
The Kharijites also often sided with the poor, peasants, workers, and the oppressed. They led some peasant uprisings against the terrible oppression that al-Ḥajjāj imposed on the people of Iraq.

There was another important feature of the Kharijite movement that had to be mentioned. Most of the religious and intellectual schools of the period fought them not only politically but also at the level of ideas. Their theory of faith—the theory from which they justified their violent struggles—came under sustained attack.
In discussing this conflict, we tried to uncover the political roots of the different theories of faith.

Our conclusion was that the huge debate which occupied intellectual life for so long—whether a person who committed a major sin should be declared an unbeliever or should remain a Muslim—had a political and partisan conflict behind it.
It was not an intellectual debate isolated from political reality.
That reality stretched from the killing of ʿUthmān through the rise of the Muʿtazila, the emergence of kalām, and eventually the development of Arab-Islamic philosophy itself.

While political conflict was developing along the lines we have described, another kind of conflict was developing alongside it. This second conflict followed much the same course, but with a degree of independence of its own. At first, it took the form of an intellectual dispute over Islamic law.

One striking feature of this legal and intellectual conflict was how deeply it was connected with the different social environments of the Arab-Islamic world.

We will see that these disagreements over legal questions became one of the forces driving the wider development of Arab-Islamic thought. Out of that development would come the rise of kalām: rational theological debate, and with it a growing form of philosophical thinking about the new questions confronting Muslim thinkers.
